payload.problem_addressed: Constructing complete programs from scratch is a major unsolved challenge for coding agents, and there is a lack of scalable training environments spanning the whole software-engineering life cycle for this from-scratch setting.
payload.method_summary: MindForge is an automated pipeline that converts open-source command-line programs into source-free training environments exposing only a compiled reference executable and its documentation, used to curate program-synthesis trajectories from a teacher agent (GLM-5.2) for fine-tuning a smaller student model (Qwen3.6-27B).
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces MindForge, a pipeline that builds source-free program-synthesis training environments from open-source CLI programs, and uses it to distill teacher-agent trajectories into a smaller model. Fine-tuning on this data raises the student's ProgramBench pass rate from 37.98% to 49.51%, matching much larger frontier models, and improves the student across seven unseen software-engineering benchmarks spanning repository generation/translation, bug fixing, and cross-language issue resolution.

payload.problem_addressed: MCTS-based Go engines (AlphaZero/MuZero-style) require heavy tree search to correct policy-network errors, which is a computational bottleneck on consumer hardware, and without deep search these models hallucinate high-confidence but strategically fatal moves.
payload.method_summary: The paper disentangles the policy head from a separate Belief head that acts as an internal simulator and independent critic modeling epistemic uncertainty and strategic stability, integrates Transformer/GRU memory for long-term dependencies (including the Ko rule), and uses a gating mechanism to filter overconfident policy errors, shifting reliance from runtime search to a learned parametric critic.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes a Belief-Guided architecture with a disentangled Belief head that serves as an internal simulator/critic distinct from the traditional value function, combined with a gating mechanism that filters overconfident policy errors. It claims this shifts the burden of intelligence from runtime MCTS search to parametric intuition, improving search-free win rates and reducing hallucinated moves, enabling professional-level play on limited hardware.

reduces high-confidence but strategically fatal move proposals (hallucination)

payload.problem_addressed: Learning-based vulnerability detectors classify functions in isolation, missing interprocedural evidence (71.7% of vulnerable functions in a CVE sample need evidence outside the function), and agentic RL lacks a reliable reward because a verdict-only reward can be earned without real investigation.
payload.method_summary: VulAgentRL builds an agentic RL framework on a Code Property Graph (CPG) that the policy queries at inference time for callers, callees, and dataflow, and that at training time verifies the evidence the policy cites via exact integer-node-ID comparison rather than textual matching, crediting only verdicts supported by graph-verifiable evidence; the policy is warm-started by distilling teacher investigations before RL.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes VulAgentRL, which uses a Code Property Graph both as a queryable evidence source at inference and as an exact, non-textual verifier of cited evidence at training time to produce a reliable RL reward. It shows a teacher-investigation distillation warm start is necessary because RL cannot acquire tool-use behavior it never samples, and demonstrates the approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, including frontier models, under a leakage-preventing repository-level split.
key_architecture_choices: Code Property Graph (CPG) used both as an inference-time queryable tool and a training-time reward verifier
exact integer-node-ID based evidence verification instead of textual matching
warm start via distillation of teacher investigation trajectories before RL
payload.headline_results: VulAgentRL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, including frontier models, on the strict pair-wise-correct metric while issuing fewer tool calls, with the advantage persisting on an out-of-distribution corpus and under class imbalance.
claimed_advantages: reward is exact/graph-verifiable rather than textual, avoiding reward hacking via a verdict-only signal
outperforms frontier-model baselines with fewer tool calls
generalizes to out-of-distribution data and class imbalance
limitations: RL cannot acquire tool-use behavior it never samples, requiring a distillation warm start

payload.problem_addressed: Standard domain-generalization methods pursue invariant causal representations, which fails when the domain itself modulates how causal content maps to the response, since feeding domain style directly into the predictor can create misleading shortcuts.
payload.method_summary: LADDER (Latent Adaptive Domain Disentanglement and Environment Reweighting) is a fixed-model domain-generalization pipeline that learns disentangled causal/style representations, freezes the encoders, fits source-specific classifiers, and at inference uses an unlabeled target-domain covariate set only to compute weights over the fixed source-specific classifiers -- with no target labels and no model-state updates -- using style to locate the unseen target domain among source domains.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes LADDER, which reframes cross-domain style variation as a signal for locating an unseen target domain among source domains rather than noise to be removed, using it to reweight a set of frozen source-specific classifiers at inference time. It provides theoretical guarantees for this source-reweighting scheme and validates it on simulations, FMoW, and a location-grouped iWildCam protocol, showing gains in overall and group-averaged accuracy over invariance-based baselines.
key_architecture_choices: disentangled causal and style representation learning
frozen encoders after training (no target-time model updates)
source-specific fixed classifiers
inference-time reweighting of classifiers using unlabeled target covariates
payload.headline_results: LADDER achieves gains in overall and group-averaged accuracy on FMoW and a location-grouped iWildCam protocol relative to invariance-based domain generalization baselines.
claimed_advantages: requires no model-state updates at deployment
comes with theoretical guarantees for the source-reweighting scheme
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core idea -- keeping a fixed, frozen model and using unlabeled target-distribution covariates only to reweight among source-specific predictors, rather than retraining or forcing domain-invariant features -- is a deployment-time technique directly applicable to hexgen's domain-gap problem: hexgen could maintain source-specific (synthetic inverse-factory vs. real auto-labeled CAD) decoding heads or verifier-tuned variants and use unlabeled real-part statistics at inference to reweight/select among them, without retraining on new real-part distributions.
payload.reviewer_notes: Only the abstract was available; details of the causal/style disentanglement mechanism and the theoretical guarantees are not grounded beyond the abstract's description. Evaluated on image/tabular domain-generalization benchmarks (FMoW, iWildCam), not CAD or geometric data, so transfer is at the algorithmic-pattern level.

provenance.method_summary: a fixed-model DG pipeline that learns causal/style representations, freezes the encoders, fits source-specific classifiers, and uses an unlabeled target-domain covariate set only at inference to compute weights over these fixed classifiers, with no target labels or model-state updates

payload.problem_addressed: Existing RL post-training for code LLMs relies on sparse outcome rewards or statically combined dense signals, even though syntax validity, executability, functional correctness, and structural organization are different, progressively dependent programming capabilities that a single flat reward or fixed weighting fails to capture well.
payload.method_summary: DHRCL decomposes reward feedback into syntax validation, execution success, unit-test pass rate, and AST-based structural similarity, organized through an automatically-timed three-stage (Syntax, Execution, Pass & Structural) curriculum, plus a stage-aware token-level credit-redistribution mechanism that emphasizes established token patterns during syntax optimization, propagates non-local execution feedback uniformly, and allocates more credit/blame to less-established tokens during final functional optimization.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces DHRCL, a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes code-generation reward into a hierarchy of dense signals (syntax, execution, unit-test pass rate, structural similarity) and schedules them through an automatically-timed curriculum rather than fixed thresholds. It further proposes stage-aware token credit redistribution following a consolidation-to-refinement principle, and shows consistent gains over binary, pass-rate, reward-model, and other verifiable dense-reward baselines across Qwen3-4B/8B/14B backbones.
key_architecture_choices: reward decomposition into syntax validation, execution success, unit-test pass rate, AST-based structural similarity
three-stage Syntax -> Execution -> Pass & Structural curriculum with automatically determined stage duration
stage-aware probability-based token credit redistribution (consolidation-to-refinement principle)
payload.headline_results: Under a unified Qwen3-8B/KodCode protocol, DHRCL outperforms binary, pass-rate, reward-model-based, and verifiable dense-reward baselines, with the advantage remaining consistent from Qwen3-4B to Qwen3-14B.
claimed_advantages: reward signal reflects progressively dependent capabilities instead of a flat/static combination
curriculum stage duration is determined automatically from validation trends, not manual thresholds
advantage is consistent as model capacity scales
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The staged reward decomposition (syntax validity -> executability -> pass/structural quality) mirrors hexgen's own layered frozen verifier (compiles -> zero inverted elements -> quality bounds -> boundary fidelity), and DHRCL's curriculum-scheduled, stage-aware credit redistribution could inform how hexgen's future RL/rejection-sampling refinement stages weight token-level credit differently depending on which verifier gate is currently the binding constraint, rather than treating the frozen verifier as a single flat pass/fail signal during any RL fine-tuning.
payload.reviewer_notes: Only the abstract was available; the exact curriculum-timing heuristic and credit-redistribution formula are not grounded beyond the high-level description given. Domain is text code LLMs (Qwen backbones), not geometric/CAD program generation, and DHRCL assumes a differentiable RL training loop rather than hexgen's current supervised-imitation + frozen-verifier screening setup.
